name: Hana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions and government. This conversation is confidential. What does a workday usually involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and still learning this junior accounting job, though I have a bachelor’s degree in accounting. I sort invoices, draft accounts and tax returns, and ask my senior reviewer to check the tax codes I miss. I use an approved AI tool now and then, after colleagues show me what it gets right and wrong. I enjoy finding the invoice that explains a mismatch, but rushed corrections near pickup time wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is going on at home this month?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Erik, my partner, drives deliveries, and our two children do homework below a damp patch in the kitchen. The roof quote is heavy beside our mortgage, my ordinary junior pay and about two months of expenses saved. There are some accounting jobs nearby, but I would rather fix the leak before risking a move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a small saving on invoice entry is welcome if the final tax figure is checked. The firm still has to answer the phone when a client cannot make sense of a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage is steady but the kitchen roof needs repair, so two months of expenses in savings does not feel generous. I earn ordinary junior pay, and a small software change will not fix the roof bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep preparing the accounts and use the approved AI tool I sometimes use for invoice sorting after my senior checks it. In the first year I would move 30 from our monthly takeaway budget into the roof account while my hours stay full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the roof and relieved that the job itself stays roughly the same. A quicker screen is nice, but it is not a new income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the roof worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is a damp patch over the children’s desk, and the repair quote is larger than our spare cash. My partner Erik and I have put a bucket there until the roofer can start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check the AI sorting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I compare each flagged invoice with the original receipt, then ask my senior reviewer about anything odd. I use the tool now and then, after others have tried it, rather than being the first person to test a new version.

say: I would welcome **faster invoice entry** if someone checks the final tax figure.
I would keep a **person on the phone** for confused clients.
think: Our **roof repair** may use much of our two-month cushion.
Small software gains do not change my **junior wage**.
do: Keep preparing **accounts** and use the approved sorter only after senior checks.
Move **30 monthly** from takeaways into the roof account while hours stay full.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the roof, with my job broadly stable.
S0.quote: A quicker screen is nice, but it is not a new income.
fieldNote: Her **roof leak** is the main baseline worry, and she sees no major job change in this mild world.
Her **occasional AI use** follows senior checking, and she directs a real spending cut into a named repair account.

steps.text: Keep preparing accounts with approved sorter after senior check
Move 30 monthly from takeaways to roof account while hours hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the office to keep one person checking tax drafts and to teach juniors what the system gets wrong. If the firm removes the learning work, the next reviewer will have little practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software may take many invoice entries and draft returns, so my hours could be cut. We have about two months saved and a roof bill coming, but there are some nearby firms and I can learn a tested system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask my senior reviewer to let me test the approved drafting tool on four old returns during paid hours, then write down each corrected item. I would pause the roof upgrade that is not needed to stop the leak; if my shifts are cut in the first year, I would apply for advertised junior tax posts nearby while keeping current paid shifts until a written offer and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible cut, especially with the roof quote. I can still see ways to protect the mortgage if the firm tells us early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly can wait on the roof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The decorative tiles can wait, but the leak repair cannot. Erik, my partner, and I would ask the roofer for separate prices so we do not delay the urgent work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the drafting tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the senior reviewer to find the same errors on those four returns and show me where I missed one. I can use a tool after it proves itself on real cases.

say: I would keep a **named checker** on automated tax drafts.
I would ask the firm to preserve **junior learning** on real returns.
think: My **invoice and draft hours** could shrink as software spreads.
A **roof bill** and two-month cushion make any hours cut hard.
do: Test **four old returns** in the approved tool during paid hours with senior review.
Delay only **decorative roof tiles**, while paying for the urgent leak repair.
After an actual cut, apply to **advertised local tax posts** while keeping shifts until a written offer and start date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost hours and a roof bill.
S1.quote: The decorative tiles can wait, but the leak repair cannot.
fieldNote: She separates **urgent repair** from cosmetic tiles, showing that her spending plan does not ignore the leak over the children’s desk.
Her **tool test** needs paid time and senior review; she keeps current wages until an external offer and start date arrive.

steps.text: Test four old tax returns in approved tool during paid hours with senior review
Delay decorative roof tiles while paying for urgent leak repair
Apply to advertised local tax posts after cut; keep shifts until written offer and start date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 changes tax and account desk work in 2028, before capable robots come around 2031. I would ask the firm to give us an honest shift plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to remove most junior draft hours once cheaper AGI can do the thinking. The roof repair and mortgage could use our two-month cushion quickly, and nearby firms might cut the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the roofer to do only the leak repair and keep the tile upgrade off the bill, then request a written roster forecast. If my shifts fall in the first year after 2028, I would apply to advertised local payroll jobs with written pay and hours at least equal to mine; if none is open, I would ask Erik whether confirmed extra delivery shifts could cover one mortgage payment while I keep any paid tax hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the household budget. A lost wage and a leaking roof could arrive together. I have steps to take, but the account balance is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Erik get those delivery shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erik drives deliveries and can sometimes cover a weekend route, but the dispatcher decides. We would count only a confirmed route, not a hopeful phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop the repair if work fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the water is near the children’s desk and could make the home worse. I would ask the roofer for staged payments on the leak repair, with the amount and dates written down.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches our tax screens before capable robots arrive.
I would request a **written shift plan** from the firm.
think: I expect most **junior draft hours** to be removed after 2028.
The **roof and mortgage** could drain our two-month cushion fast.
do: Request **leak-only repair** and written staged payment dates from the roofer.
After lost shifts, apply to **advertised local payroll jobs** with written equal pay and hours.
If none opens, ask **partner Erik** about confirmed delivery shifts while keeping paid tax hours.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely income loss alongside the roof bill.
S2.quote: A lost wage and a leaking roof could arrive together.
fieldNote: The **robot delay** is irrelevant to her desk-based drafts; she expects junior hours to disappear when AGI arrives.
She keeps the **urgent repair** but seeks written stages, and counts Erik’s delivery income only after a route is confirmed.

steps.text: Order leak-only repair and request written staged payment dates
Apply to advertised local payroll jobs after cuts with written equal pay and hours
Ask partner Erik about confirmed delivery shifts while retaining paid tax hours if no vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues AGI by 2031 gives us a few years to learn which tax checks still need an accountant. The robots around 2034 are later than the office change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let us finish the roof and build back savings before draft work shrinks. I would want to learn payroll because I already see wage entries in client accounts, but I would need paid training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager for a paid payroll course and enrol only if the fees and study hours are approved in writing. I would rebuild three months of expenses after the leak is repaired, adding 80 a month while both wages hold; in the first year after 2031, if draft hours fall, I would take a vacant payroll post only with written salary and hours at least equal to my present job, or keep tax shifts while applying to advertised nearby jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though a few years gives us time to finish the roof first. I would still need a real payroll vacancy, not just a course certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses to pay for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise wage reconciliations on old files with my senior reviewer during current paid hours if she agrees. I would not use roof money for tuition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you rebuild the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the leak is paid, we would keep skipping takeaways and set an automatic transfer on payday. If either wage falls, we would pause the 80 transfer.

say: I would use the **2031 runway** to learn paid payroll work.
I would tell colleagues the **2034 robots** do not delay office changes.
think: Draft work may **shrink in 2031**, after we finish the roof.
I need **paid training** before payroll is a credible option.
do: Enrol in a **payroll course** with written fees and paid hours; otherwise practise old wage files if my senior agrees.
Rebuild **three months of expenses** with 80 monthly while both wages hold after the leak is paid.
After lost draft hours, take a **vacant payroll post** with written equal salary and hours, or apply nearby while employed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about income and the need for a real opening.
S3.quote: I would still need a real payroll vacancy, not just a course certificate.
fieldNote: The **roof is first**: she starts saving again only after the urgent repair is paid.
If the course is **unfunded**, she seeks supervised wage reconciliation on old files during paid hours rather than spending repair money.

steps.text: Enrol in payroll course only with written fees and paid study hours
Save 80 monthly after leak is paid while both wages hold
Take vacant payroll work with written equal pay/hours after cuts or apply nearby while employed
Practise old wage files during paid hours if senior agrees and course is unfunded

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives the firm a decade to make a fair training plan and families time to lower debt. The accounts desk still faces thinking AI in 2036, before robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could finish the roof, build six months of expenses and maybe reduce the mortgage balance if wages stay steady. I would still expect routine draft returns to vanish by 2036, but I could be checking harder client questions then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep preparing returns and ask the senior reviewer for one paid client-query shift a month, if the manager approves it. After the roof is paid, I would save 100 a month until we have six months of expenses while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036 I would take a vacant paid client-support role only with written salary and hours at least equal to now, or keep any return shifts while applying for advertised local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change, though the next few years look more secure. A decade is enough to fix the roof and test a client role without dropping my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the monthly query shift teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise asking a client for missing invoices while the senior reviewer listens, then correct the return together. I need more experience before I can own the call alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay down the mortgage before savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after the roof and the six-month cash buffer. A smaller loan balance would be nice, but it will not cover an unexpected repair bill next winter.

say: I would ask for a **fair training plan** before 2036.
I would note the **accounts desk** changes before capable robots arrive.
think: Steady wages could fund **roof repair** and a six-month cash buffer.
do: Keep **preparing returns** and learn client calls in an approved paid monthly shift.
After roof repair, save **100 monthly** toward six months of expenses while both wages hold.
Take a **vacant paid client-support role** with written equal salary and hours, or apply locally while employed.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about 2036 while near-term work looks secure.
S4.quote: I need more experience before I can own the call alone.
fieldNote: Her **longer runway** supports a sequence: repair the roof, rebuild cash, then consider mortgage principal payments.
She wants **supervised client calls** during paid time; moving roles still depends on a vacancy with written equivalent salary and hours.

steps.text: Keep preparing tax returns while shifts remain
Learn client calls in paid monthly shift if manager approves and senior supervises
Save 100 monthly after roof repair while both wages hold until six months cash
Take vacant paid client-support role with written equal pay and hours or apply locally while employed

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my draft hours could go while the roof still leaks. A written shift plan, paid payroll training and a real vacancy with clear wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether the roof can wait for a career plan. The damp patch above the children’s desk will not read a staffing forecast.

headlineQuote: The damp patch above the children’s desk will not read a staffing forecast.
portrait: At **43**, Hana is a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree, still learning account and tax reviews.
She and **partner Erik** have two school-age children, a mortgage, ordinary junior pay and two months saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** after colleagues test it; a leaking kitchen roof already pressures the household budget.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her; longer runways allow paid payroll learning, roof repair and conditional savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase her junior draft hours while the roof repair and mortgage drain their cushion.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **written shift plan**, paid payroll training and a real vacancy with clear wages.
